ai-at-work.title: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
ai-at-work.excerpt: OpenAI will introduce a single usage meter across ChatGPT as it combines the Chat and Work experiences.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: OpenAI is merging its ChatGPT Chat and Work products into one unified experience, which means power users will share a single usage quota instead of having separate limits for each. This matters because plenty of organizations have built workflows around ChatGPT's work tier, and now they'll need to rethink how they allocate tokens across their teams. Honestly, this feels like a classic move of combining products to simplify the backend while quietly making heavy users pay more or complain louder, which is basically the tech industry playbook at this point.

ai-at-work.title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
ai-at-work.excerpt: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei pushes back against rivals’ accusations that he favors surrendering human agency to AI, even as leading AI companies increasingly automate their own research and model devel
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Anthropic's CEO is pushing back against claims that his company wants to hand over human control to AI systems, even though Anthropic is literally automating its own research and development work right now. This matters because if the people building AI can't be straight about what they're actually doing with automation, how are enterprises supposed to make informed decisions about deploying these tools in their own organizations? Look, I've seen a lot of defensive posturing in tech, but calling concerns about automated AI development "absurd" while actively automating AI development is a new standard for having your cake and eating it too.

ai-at-work.title: Want to buy your kid an AI toy this Christmas? Not in New York
ai-at-work.excerpt: New York has banned AI chatbot toys for five years as new research from Common Sense Media reveals troubling safety failures, including exposure to inappropriate content and risks to emotional develop
ai-at-work.dwp_take: New York just slapped a five-year ban on AI chatbot toys after research showed these things expose kids to inappropriate content and potentially mess with their emotional development. For digital workplace folks, this matters because it signals regulators are finally getting serious about AI safety and liability, which means your enterprise AI initiatives are about to face actual scrutiny instead of just hand-waving. Honestly, if a toy AI can't stay on the rails, maybe we should all pump the brakes on deploying conversational AI everywhere and actually testing it first.

ai-at-work.title: AI data centers are becoming harder to build, and neoclouds are feeling it
ai-at-work.excerpt: ⁠Nvidia has made clear⁠ it won’t backstop an AI data center until it’s nearly ready to run, and that’s landing just as neoclouds report construction delays and more expensive debt. The message to deve
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Nvidia is tightening its support for AI data center projects, refusing to commit funding until facilities are nearly operational, which is hitting neocloud companies with construction delays and higher borrowing costs. This matters because it signals a fundamental shift in how infrastructure gets built: execution and hard assets now trump startup promises and venture hype. For digital workplace folks, this is a reality check that the AI tools flooding your platforms require unglamorous physical infrastructure that takes time, money, and genuine competence to build.

tools-tech.title: Gen Z is the least interested in AI at work – and it’s not even close
tools-tech.excerpt: Younger workers don’t find AI useful, according to a recent survey.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Gen Z workers are significantly less enthusiastic about AI tools at work compared to older generations, with the survey showing they find limited practical value in current AI applications. This matters because it challenges the assumption that digital natives automatically embrace every new tech trend, and it signals that vendors need to actually solve real problems instead of just slapping AI onto everything. Here's the thing: Gen Z didn't grow up watching PowerPoint presentations about the future, they lived through it, and they're not impressed by solutions looking for problems.

tools-tech.title: Anthropic lets you install Claude ‘artifacts’ as Mac apps
tools-tech.excerpt: Anthropic is now rolling out beta access to a new Claude feature that lets you save some of what it does as live apps on Macs, using “artifacts.” What’s new is that you can take an artifact and instal
tools-tech.dwp_take: Anthropic now lets Claude users save AI-generated outputs as standalone Mac and Windows apps instead of keeping them trapped in the chat interface. This matters because knowledge workers are quietly building real tools through AI, and having them live as actual applications means they're more likely to get used repeatedly and integrated into actual workflows. I've seen 30 years of promising tech languish because it stayed buried in the wrong interface, so giving these artifacts proper app status might actually be the difference between a parlor trick and something people rely on.

digital-culture.title: How job hunting became an expensive cash suck
digital-culture.excerpt: There’s an expense that’s easy to overlook when talking about the cost of living: getting and keeping a job. We tend to think of work as the thing that pays the bills, but commuting and the other cost
digital-culture.dwp_take: Job hunting and employment are now carrying hidden costs that eat into worker paychecks before they even start, from commuting to interview prep to relocation fees. This matters because it's creating a silent barrier to employment, particularly for lower-income workers who can't absorb these upfront expenses, and it's something most organizations completely ignore when talking about "accessible" hiring. The irony is that companies complaining about talent shortages haven't considered that some people literally can't afford to work for them anymore.

digital-culture.title: Why employees are ‘habit hugging’ at work
digital-culture.excerpt: If you’re prone to hanging on to the way things always used to be done at work, you might be “habit hugging.” It’s where employees hold on to familiar routines even after new tools and processes have
digital-culture.dwp_take: Employees are sticking with old work habits even after new tools and processes roll out, a phenomenon researchers are calling "habit hugging." This matters because it explains why your expensive new collaboration platform sits unused while people email spreadsheets around like it's 2003. The real insight here isn't that change is hard, it's that most organizations introduce new tools without actually addressing the underlying anxiety and loss of control employees feel, so of course they hug their old habits like a security blanket.

digital-culture.title: Can potential clients find you using AI?
digital-culture.excerpt: A few months ago, I got a DM on LinkedIn from someone wanting to interview me for a feature she was writing. At the end of the interview, I asked her how she found me. She replied, “ChatGPT.” If you’r
digital-culture.dwp_take: A journalist found a source for her Fast Company article by asking ChatGPT to recommend experts, which led to a LinkedIn DM. This matters because it shows how AI is fundamentally changing client discovery and lead generation, meaning your digital footprint now needs to be "findable" by algorithms, not just people. The real kicker is that most solopreneurs are still optimizing for Google when they should be worried about whether ChatGPT even knows they exist.

digital-culture.title: Some people don’t use AI at work—and feel judged for it
digital-culture.excerpt: New workplace fear unlocked—and it’s not being yelled at for heated-up fish in the office microwave or getting too merry at the Christmas party. As companies continue to invest billions in their AI st
digital-culture.dwp_take: Companies are creating a new workplace anxiety where employees worry about being judged for not using AI enough, with nearly half of workers expressing this concern according to a recent LSE report. This matters because it signals that digital workplace leaders are failing at change management, pushing technology adoption without building the culture and psychological safety needed for people to actually embrace it. The irony is delicious: we're supposed to be making work more human with AI, but instead we're just adding another reason for people to feel like they're not measuring up.

industry-news.title: Nvidia 621.40 Targets SSD-Writing Bug: Which GPUs Are Affected?
industry-news.excerpt: Nvidia's 621.40 driver includes another fix for excessive SSD writes after its earlier hotfix left some users reporting problems. Here's which GPUs have reports and how to check your system. The post
industry-news.dwp_take: Nvidia released driver 621.40 to fix an SSD-writing bug that was hammering storage drives, following an earlier hotfix that apparently made things worse for some users. If your organization runs GPU-heavy workloads for AI, rendering, or data processing, driver stability directly impacts your infrastructure costs and uptime, so this matters. Nothing says "we fixed it" quite like needing two attempts to solve the same problem, but at least they're persistent.

industry-news.title: Google Search Can Now Access Your Wallet Data: How Personal Intelligence Works
industry-news.excerpt: Google Search can now use connected Wallet data to personalize financial advice. Here's how to enable the feature, what Google does with your information, and which privacy settings to review. The pos
industry-news.dwp_take: Google Search is now tapping into your Wallet data to serve up personalized financial advice, which means the search giant wants deeper access to your personal transaction history. For digital workplace pros, this matters because employees using Google Workspace need to understand what data they're exposing and how it flows through their organization's tech stack, especially if compliance and data governance are part of their job. Personally, I'm waiting for the day Google offers to just manage my finances directly because apparently asking permission feels so 2015.

industry-news.title: Claude Turns Artifacts Into Desktop Apps: What Changes on Mac and Windows
industry-news.excerpt: Claude can turn artifacts into Mac and Windows apps. Learn what permissions they can request, what IT can control, and how to run a pilot with limited access. The post Claude Turns Artifacts Into Desk
industry-news.dwp_take: Anthropic's Claude can now package AI-generated code artifacts directly into standalone desktop applications for Mac and Windows, with granular permission controls that let IT teams manage what these apps can access. This matters because it collapses the gap between AI experimentation and actual tool deployment, meaning your users might start building and distributing custom applications without traditional software governance workflows. The real question isn't whether this is cool (it is), but whether your IT team is ready for employees to become accidental software publishers.

Honestly, if your company's still worried about foldables being "gimmicks," you're about five years behind where the hardware conversation actually is.
